questions.question: What are the differences between HashMap, TreeMap, and LinkedHashMap?
questions.title: Map Implementations Comparison
questions.direct_answer: HashMap gives no key ordering (O(1)); LinkedHashMap preserves insertion or access order (O(1)); TreeMap sorts keys (O(log n)).

interviewer_intent.testing: Map implementation selection and performance trade-offs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking LinkedHashMap maintains sorted order (it's insertion order, not sorted)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention LinkedHashMap's access-order mode (LRU cache) and TreeMap's NavigableMap methods

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So Java has three main Map implementations for different ordering needs.

HashMap: the default choice. O(1) average for get/put, no ordering. When you just need key-value lookup and don't care about iteration order, use HashMap.

LinkedHashMap: same O(1) performance as HashMap but maintains insertion order by default. When you iterate, you get entries in the order they were added. There's also an 'access order' mode where recently accessed entries move to the end — this is the basis for LRU caches (override removeEldestEntry()).

TreeMap: keys are sorted — either by natural ordering (Comparable) or a custom Comparator. O(log n) for operations. Useful when you need keys in sorted order, or when you need NavigableMap methods like firstKey(), lastKey(), subMap(from, to), higherKey(), floorKey(). Doesn't allow null keys.

speakable_v2.hook: Three Map implementations, three ordering stories: none, insertion order, or sorted — and the ordering choice costs you speed.

groups.heading: HashMap
groups.text: Default Map. O(1) average for get and put. No guaranteed key ordering — iteration order is unpredictable. One null key allowed. Fastest option when you only need key-value lookup.

groups.heading: LinkedHashMap
groups.text: Same O(1) performance as HashMap but maintains insertion order by default. Entries come out in the order they were added. An access-order mode moves recently accessed entries to the end — the basis for LRU caches.

items: HashMap: product ID to product object lookup — you don't care about iteration order, just speed.
LinkedHashMap: API response that must return entries in the order they were inserted — same O(1) speed, guaranteed order.
TreeMap: products sorted by ID for a report, or range query to find all products with IDs between 100 and 200 using subMap().

beats.text: candidates miss: LinkedHashMap doesn't sort keys — it preserves insertion order. These are completely different things. TreeMap sorts alphabetically or by Comparator; LinkedHashMap just remembers which entry came first.

speakable_v2.cap: HashMap for speed, LinkedHashMap for predictable iteration order, TreeMap for sorted keys or range queries — pick based on what iteration behavior you need.

questions.question: How can you implement a simple LRU cache using LinkedHashMap?
questions.title: LRU Cache with LinkedHashMap
questions.direct_answer: Create a LinkedHashMap with access-order=true and override removeEldestEntry() to return true when size exceeds the capacity limit.

seo.metaTitle: LRU Cache Using LinkedHashMap in Java
seo.metaDescription: Implement LRU cache in Java using LinkedHashMap — access-order mode and removeEldestEntry override.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app storing a list of products and looking them up by ID
familiarity_anchors: a browser cache that evicts the least recently visited page
LRU as 'evict the oldest untouched entry'
speakable_v2.hook: LinkedHashMap's access-order mode plus one overridden method gives you a working LRU cache in about ten lines.

beats.text: An LRU (Least Recently Used) cache evicts the entry that was accessed least recently when it's full. LinkedHashMap supports this natively through an access-order constructor flag — when set to true, every get or put moves the accessed entry to the end of the linked order. The entry at the head is always the least recently used.

LinkedHashMap was designed with exactly this pattern in mind. The removeEldestEntry hook was added as an extension point specifically for LRU caches — Java's designers anticipated the use case and made it a protected method you can override.

items: Constructor: super(capacity, 0.75f, true) — the third argument enables access-order mode.
removeEldestEntry override: return size() > capacity — evicts the head entry when the map is full.
get() and put() automatically move the accessed entry to the tail — most recently used is always at the back.
Thread safety: this implementation is not thread-safe — wrap with Collections.synchronizedMap() for concurrent use.

beats.text: non-obvious: without the access-order flag (default insertion order), get() doesn't reorder entries — the cache evicts the oldest inserted entry, not the least recently accessed. That's a different eviction policy (FIFO, not LRU). Always pass true as the third constructor argument for true LRU behavior.

items: Default LinkedHashMap uses insertion order — you need access-order=true for LRU eviction. Forgetting this flag gives you FIFO, not LRU.
The LinkedHashMap LRU cache is single-threaded — for concurrent use, consider a synchronized wrapper or a dedicated concurrent LRU implementation.

speakable_v2.cap: LRU cache in Java: extend LinkedHashMap, pass access-order=true, override removeEldestEntry — three steps, ten lines, done.

questions.question: What are the NavigableMap methods in TreeMap and when are they useful?
questions.title: TreeMap NavigableMap Methods
questions.direct_answer: TreeMap's NavigableMap methods — floorKey(), ceilingKey(), higherKey(), lowerKey(), headMap(), tailMap(), subMap() — enable range queries and nearest-neighbor lookups.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using TreeMap only as a sorted alternative to HashMap without knowing the range query methods
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete use case: stock price closest to target, events in a time range

sections.title: Key Points
content: lowerKey(k): largest key < k, higherKey(k): smallest key > k
subMap(from, to): entries between from (inclusive) and to (exclusive)
Use case: find closest stock price, all events in a time window

followup_questions: How do you get all keys in a range from TreeMap?

seo.metaDescription: TreeMap NavigableMap methods — floorKey, ceilingKey, headMap, tailMap, subMap with practical examples.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app storing a list of products and looking them up by ID
familiarity_anchors: finding the closest bus stop to your location
a sorted price list with range queries
speakable_v2.hook: TreeMap isn't just a sorted HashMap — its NavigableMap methods let you find nearest keys and query ranges in O(log n).

beats.text: TreeMap implements NavigableMap which adds methods for nearest-neighbor and range lookups that are only possible because the keys are sorted. These operations run in O(log n) using the underlying red-black tree structure. HashMap has none of these — you'd need to iterate all entries, which is O(n).

Range and neighbor queries are common in real applications — stock prices nearest a target, events in a time window, cache keys between two bounds. Sorted data stored in a tree enables these in O(log n) without any extra scan.

items: floorKey(k): returns the largest key that is less than or equal to k — closest key at or below target.
ceilingKey(k): returns the smallest key that is greater than or equal to k — closest key at or above target.
lowerKey(k): strictly less than k. higherKey(k): strictly greater than k.
headMap(k): sub-map view of all entries with keys strictly less than k.
tailMap(k): sub-map view of all entries with keys greater than or equal to k.
subMap(from, to): sub-map from from (inclusive) to to (exclusive).

beats.text: non-obvious: in the product catalog app, if product IDs are stored in a TreeMap, you can find all products with IDs between 1000 and 2000 with a single subMap(1000, 2000) call — no loop, no filtering. For a pricing engine, floorKey(targetPrice) finds the closest price at or below the target in O(log n).

items: headMap, tailMap, and subMap return live views — modifications to the view modify the original TreeMap and vice versa. Use new TreeMap<>(sub) for an independent copy.
floorKey and ceilingKey return null if no qualifying key exists — always null-check the result.

speakable_v2.cap: TreeMap's NavigableMap methods make it a powerful tool for sorted data, range queries, and nearest-key lookups — well beyond simple sorted iteration.

questions.question: What are the modern Map methods — getOrDefault(), computeIfAbsent(), and merge()?
questions.title: Modern Map Methods
questions.direct_answer: getOrDefault() returns a fallback for missing keys; computeIfAbsent() computes and stores a value if absent; merge() combines existing and new values with a function.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using map.put(key, map.getOrDefault(key, 0) + 1) when map.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum) is cleaner
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the frequency counting pattern with merge() — it's much more readable than the old pattern

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So Java 8 added several Map methods that replace common verbose patterns.

`getOrDefault(key, defaultValue)` — returns defaultValue if key is absent. Much cleaner than `map.containsKey(key) ? map.get(key) : default`.

`computeIfAbsent(key, k -> computeValue(k))` — if key is absent, computes and stores the value, then returns it. Classic use: grouping. `map.computeIfAbsent(word, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(occurrence)` — creates list if needed, then adds.

`merge(key, value, (existing, newVal) -> combined)` — if key absent, stores value. If present, combines existing with new value using the function. Frequency counting: `map.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum)` — adds 1 if absent, or increments if present. Much cleaner than the getOrDefault pattern.

`compute(key, (k, v) -> newValue)` — the most general version; v is null if key absent.

seo.metaTitle: Java Map getOrDefault, computeIfAbsent, merge Methods
seo.metaDescription: Modern Java Map methods — getOrDefault, computeIfAbsent, merge, and compute with practical examples.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app storing a list of products and looking them up by ID
familiarity_anchors: one-liner shortcuts replacing verbose if-else patterns
Java 8 API upgrades for cleaner code
speakable_v2.hook: Three Java 8 Map methods that each replace a common multi-line pattern — knowing them signals modern Java fluency.

beats.text: Java 8 added getOrDefault, computeIfAbsent, and merge to Map — each replacing a common verbose pattern with a single atomic method call. They're cleaner, safer, and in many cases more efficient than the pre-Java-8 equivalent because they avoid duplicate key lookups.

The old patterns — containsKey then get, get then null check then put — always made two or three separate map lookups. The new methods do the check-and-act atomically in one call, which is both cleaner and eliminates the redundant lookup.

items: getOrDefault(key, fallback): returns fallback if key is absent. Replaces the ternary map.containsKey(k) ? map.get(k) : fallback.
computeIfAbsent(key, k -> value): computes and stores the value only if key is absent, then returns it. Classic grouping pattern: map.computeIfAbsent(category, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(product).
merge(key, value, merger): if key absent, stores value. If present, applies merger(existingValue, value). Frequency counting: map.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum) — one line instead of three.
compute(key, (k, v) -> newValue): the general version; v is null when key is absent — handle both insert and update in one lambda.

beats.text: non-obvious: map.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum) is not just cleaner than map.put(word, map.getOrDefault(word, 0) + 1) — it's also one map lookup instead of two. In a product catalog app counting page views per product, the merge version is both more readable and faster at scale.

items: computeIfAbsent returns the existing or newly computed value — use it as a one-step get-or-create, not just a conditional put.
merge with a null-returning merger removes the key entirely — be careful if your combiner function can return null.

speakable_v2.cap: Master merge for frequency counting, computeIfAbsent for grouping, and getOrDefault for safe reads — three patterns that cover most Java 8 Map interview questions.
